explanation: Anomalies in sex chromosome number (inheriting too many or too few) are much better tolerated in humans than autosomal abnormalities. This tolerance exists because normal females undergo X-inactivation, where one of the two X chromosomes is deactivated to become a Barr Body. Because of this, an extra or missing X chromosome does not result in a severe gene dosage imbalance. Two major examples of sex chromosome disorders are Turner Syndrome and Klinefelter Syndrome.

questions.q: Why are abnormal numbers of sex chromosomes better tolerated in humans than abnormal numbers of autosomes?
opts: Sex chromosomes do not encode any functional proteins.
In females, one X chromosome is normally deactivated into a Barr Body, which minimizes the impact of an extra or missing X.
Sex chromosomes are degraded by the proteasome during replication.
The SRY gene prevents sex chromosomes from causing syndromic symptoms.
questions.exp: Option B is correct because the slide notes: 'In normal females, even with two X, one gets deactivated, and functions as a Barr Body... Extra X or missing X therefore does not have as great an effect.'

questions.q: Which two sex chromosome disorders are introduced on this slide?
questions.exp: Option C is correct because the slide lists 'Turner Syndrome' and 'Klinefelter Syndrome' as the 'Two main sex chromosome disorders (but not only two).'
